lines.text: Welcome to the drawing board. We start with the very first construction.
The word for today is bisect.
Bisect means to cut something into two equal parts.
Bi means two. Sect means cut. Cut into two.
Now here is the rule that surprises everybody.
You may not use your ruler to find the middle. That is measuring, not constructing.
When the exam says construct, it means use a compass, and leave your arcs on the paper.
Never rub out your arcs. Those arcs are your working, and they carry marks.
First we need a line to cut.
Slide the T-square to where you want it and draw a line one hundred and forty long.
Put a small dot at each end.
Letter the left end A, and the right end B.
We call it line AB.
Take the compass and open it to more than half the line.
The line is one hundred and forty. Half is seventy. So open it bigger than seventy.
I am using ninety. Any size over seventy will work.
Why more than half? Because if it is less, the two arcs will never reach each other.
And now the rule that matters most today. Do not touch that screw again.
The opening must stay exactly the same for all four arcs.
Put the sharp needle point exactly on A.
Press it in a little so it cannot slip.
Swing an arc above the line.
Hold the compass by the top knob only. Never hold the legs.
Now swing another arc below the line, from the same point A.
Make them long. A short arc will miss the one coming the other way.
Move the needle to B. Do not change the opening.
Swing an arc above, crossing the first one.
Look at that. The two arcs cut each other. Mark that crossing.
Now swing an arc below as well.
Call the top crossing C, and the bottom crossing D.
Join C to D with a straight line.
Where it crosses AB, call that point M.
M is the exact middle. Measure it if you like. Seventy each side.
But look at the corner where the two lines meet.
It is a right angle. Ninety degrees, perfectly square.
So one construction gave you two things. The middle, and a perpendicular.
That is why its full name is the perpendicular bisector.
Here is a line, and a point sitting on it.
We must stand a new line straight up from that point.
Straight up means at ninety degrees. We call that perpendicular.
You could cheat with a set square. But the exam says construct.
So we do it with the compass only, and we leave the arcs showing.
And notice the point is on the line. That matters. There is a different method when it is not.
Put the needle on P.
Open the compass to any small size. Forty is comfortable.
Swing a short arc that cuts the line on the left.
Without changing anything, swing one on the right too.
Call them C and D.
C and D are now exactly the same distance from P, one each side.
That is the whole trick. P is already the middle of C and D.
Now open the compass wider. Bigger than half of C to D.
And here is the nice part. You already know what to do.
This is just bisecting the line C D, which you learned yesterday.
Needle on C, swing an arc above.
Needle on D, same opening, swing an arc that crosses it.
Mark the crossing. Call it E.
Join E to P, and carry the line a little past.
That is your perpendicular.
Look at the corners. Ninety degrees on the left, ninety on the right.
Stand your set square against it to check. It should sit flat with no gap.
One warning. Do not join E to C or E to D. That is not the answer.
The answer goes through P, because P is the point you were given.
Today we cut one line into seven equal parts.
Your first thought is to measure. Let us try it.
The line is two hundred and twenty long. Divide by seven.
You get thirty-one point four two eight, and it never ends.
You cannot set that on a rule. So measuring fails.
The construction does not care. It gives seven exact parts every time.
And it works for nine parts, or thirteen, or any number you like.
From A, draw a light line going up at any angle you like.
Listen to that. Any angle. It genuinely does not matter.
I use thirty degrees because my set square gives it to me instantly.
Make it long enough to hold seven marks.
This is a construction line, so keep it light. 2H pencil.
Set your compass to any convenient size.
Needle on A, mark the sloping line once.
Move the needle into that mark and step again.
Keep walking up the line. Three. Four. Five.
Six. And seven.
Seven equal spaces, because you never changed the compass.
Number them one to seven as you go, or you will lose count.
Now join the seventh mark straight down to B.
This one line is the key to the whole construction.
Every line we draw parallel to it will cut AB in the same proportion.
That is a rule of similar triangles, and it is always true.
Now line your set square up with that closing line.
Hold the T-square hard against it so the angle cannot change.
Slide the set square down to mark six, and draw a parallel to AB.
Slide to mark five. Draw again.
Keep sliding and drawing. Four. Three. Two. One.
Do not lift the T-square between lines, or they stop being parallel.
Look where the parallels land on AB.
Seven equal parts. Measure any one and they all match.
And we never once divided two hundred and twenty by seven.
Now the second half of the title. Proportional parts.
Suppose the question says divide AB in the ratio two to five.
Two plus five is seven. So divide into seven, exactly as we did.
Then take the second mark along.
Two parts on the left, five on the right. That is your ratio.
Last time our point was sitting on the line.
This time it is floating above it.
We must drop a line from P straight down onto AB, at ninety degrees.
The word is drop, because we are coming down onto the line.
And there is a second reason this matters.
That perpendicular is the shortest distance from P to the line.
Any other line from P to AB is longer. Every single one.
Needle on P.
Now open the compass wide enough to reach past the line.
Swing an arc that cuts the line in two places.
Two places. Not one. If it only touches at one point, open wider and do it again.
Call the two cuts C and D.
C and D are the same distance from P, because they are both on the same arc.
Now it is the same old bisection again.
Needle on C, swing an arc below the line.
Needle on D, same opening, cross it.
Notice we are working below the line, on the far side from P.
That is on purpose. The further apart your two points, the straighter your join.
Call the crossing E.
Now join P all the way down to E.
It must pass through both of them. Line the rule up on both before you draw.
Where it crosses AB, mark the point. Call it F.
That corner is ninety degrees.
And the length from P down to F is the shortest distance from P to the line.
In the exam that is often the real question. Find the distance from the point to the line.
Parallel lines run beside each other and never meet.
The distance between them is the same everywhere. That is the test.
Here is a line, and a point above it.
We must draw a line through P that is parallel to AB.
There are two ways, and you should know both.
One is fast and uses the set square. One is slower and uses the compass.
First the fast way, which you will use every day.
Lay one edge of the set square exactly along the line AB.
Now slide the T-square up until it touches the set square, and hold it there.
The T-square is now a track. It cannot move.
Slide the set square along that track until its edge reaches P.
The edge is still pointing the same way, because the track is straight.
Draw. That line is parallel.
One rule. Your left hand holds the T-square down the whole time. If it shifts, start again.
Now the compass way. Use this when the exam says construct.
First we need the gap. That is the perpendicular distance from P down to the line.
You already know how to find it. Drop a perpendicular from P.
Here it is sixty-five millimetres.
Set your compass to exactly that. Sixty-five.
Do not change it again.
Pick any point on the line, well over to the left.
Needle there, and swing an arc above.
Now pick another point well over to the right.
Same opening. Swing another arc above.
Put them far apart. Two arcs close together give a wobbly answer.
Now lay your rule so it just touches the top of both arcs.
Just touching. It must not cut into them.
When a line touches a curve at one point only, we say it is tangent to it.
Draw the line.
Look where it goes. Straight through P.
And it is exactly sixty-five from AB everywhere along its length.
That is your parallel, and every arc is still on the paper as your working.
We already cut a line in half. Now we cut an angle in half.
First we need an angle. Draw a horizontal line with your T-square.
Put a dot at the left end and call it V, for vertex.
The vertex is the corner. It is where the two arms meet.
Now take the thirty sixty set square and draw the second arm at sixty degrees.
Two arms and a corner. That is an angle.
Put the needle on the vertex.
Open the compass to any comfortable size. It really does not matter.
Swing one arc that cuts across both arms.
It crosses the bottom arm here. Call it P.
And the top arm here. Call it Q.
P and Q are now the same distance from V. That is the whole idea.
Move the needle to P.
Swing a small arc inside the angle.
Now the needle to Q. Do not change the opening.
Swing another arc, crossing the first.
Mark the crossing. Call it R.
Draw a line from V, through R, and carry on past.
That is the bisector.
Check it. Sixty was the angle. Now there is thirty on this side.
And thirty on this side.
Thirty and thirty make sixty. It works.
And we never touched a protractor.
Bisect the thirty and you get fifteen. Bisect again, seven and a half.
That is how you build angles a protractor cannot read.
You own a protractor. So why learn this?
Two reasons, and both matter.
First, a protractor is a guess. You read it to about half a degree, if your eyes are good.
A construction is exact. Sixty degrees is exactly sixty.
Second, the exam often bans it. It will say construct, without a protractor.
Today we build sixty, one hundred and twenty, thirty, ninety and forty-five.
Sixty degrees comes free from any circle. Watch.
Needle on V, swing an arc that crosses the line.
Now move the needle to C. Keep exactly the same opening.
Swing again, and cut the first arc.
Join V to that crossing.
That angle is sixty degrees. Exactly sixty, every time.
Why? Because you have just built an equilateral triangle. Three equal sides, three equal angles.
One hundred and eighty divided by three is sixty.
Now do not change the compass at all.
Move the needle into the sixty degree crossing.
Swing once more, further round the arc.
Join V to that.
Sixty plus sixty. One hundred and twenty degrees.
Every step round the arc adds another sixty. Step again and you would have one hundred and eighty.
Thirty is just half of sixty, so we bisect.
Needle on C, swing an arc inside the angle.
Needle on the sixty degree point, same opening, cross it.
Join V through the crossing. That is thirty degrees.
Now think about what halving can and cannot reach.
From sixty you get thirty, fifteen, seven and a half.
You will never reach twenty or forty by halving. That is worth knowing before an exam.
Now move along to the second vertex, W.
Ninety degrees is nothing new. It is a perpendicular at a point on a line.
Step the same distance each side of W.
Then open wider and bisect between those two points.
Join W to the crossing. That is ninety degrees.
Last one. Forty-five is half of ninety, so we bisect again.
Arc from W cutting both arms.
Equal arcs from those two cuts, crossing in the middle.
Join W through, and there is forty-five.
Now look back over the whole sheet.
Sixty. One hundred and twenty. Thirty. Ninety. Forty-five.
One compass, no protractor, and every one of them exact.
Here is an angle at V.
And here is a new line at W, with no angle on it yet.
The job is to copy the angle from V onto W.
And here is what makes it interesting.
You are not told what the angle is. You never find out.
You do not need to. The compass carries it across for you.
Set the compass to any size and put the needle on V.
Swing an arc across both arms of the original angle.
Call the cuts P and Q.
Now carry that same compass across to W. Do not change it.
Swing the same arc there. It cuts the new line at one point.
Same radius at both corners. That is what makes the copy exact.
Now change the compass. Open it to the gap from P to Q.
Needle in one, pencil in the other. That is all.
That straight gap across the arc has a name. It is called a chord.
And here is the idea of the whole lesson.
For a given radius, one chord means one angle. Always.
So if you carry the chord across, you carry the angle across.
Take the compass to X on the new line.
Swing a small arc that cuts the arc you drew at W.
Mark that crossing. Call it Y.
Now join W to Y, and carry it on.
Put the two angles side by side and look at them.
They are identical. And you still do not know what they measure.
That is copying an angle.
Here is an arc. Just the curve, nothing else.
Somebody drew it, then rubbed out the centre.
Your job is to find where the compass point was.
This is not a made-up exam question. It is a real workshop job.
A casting arrives broken, with a curved edge, and you must find its radius.
You find the centre first. Then you measure out to the curve, and that is the radius.
Pick any three points on the curve.
Anywhere at all. Do not measure them.
But spread them out. Three points bunched together give a poor answer.
Call them A, B and C.
Now join A to B, and B to C, with straight lines.
Each straight line across a curve is a chord. You met that word last lesson.
Now bisect the chord A B. You know exactly how.
Equal arcs from A and from B, above and below.
Join the two crossings.
Here is the rule that makes this whole lesson work.
The perpendicular bisector of a chord always runs through the centre of the circle.
Always. So the centre is somewhere on this line.
We do not know where yet. We just know it is on it.
Now do exactly the same to the chord B C.
Equal arcs from B and from C.
Join those crossings too.
So now the centre is on this line as well.
And if it is on both lines, there is only one place it can be.
Look where the two bisectors cross.
That is the centre. Call it O.
Now check it, because you should always check.
Put the needle on O and open the compass out to A.
Swing right round.
It runs straight through B and through C, and along the whole curve.
It fits. So O is the centre, and that opening is the radius.
If it does not fit, one of your arcs slipped. Do it again.
Today we draw three shapes. A triangle, a square and a hexagon.
All three start the same way. With a circle.
Why? Because every corner sits on the circle, so every corner is the same distance from the middle.
That is what makes a shape regular. All sides equal, all angles equal.
Draw three circles, all the same size, with their centre lines.
Now we cut each one up a different way.
Start with the hexagon. Hex means six.
This is the shape of every nut and every bolt head, so you will draw it often.
Here is the beautiful part.
The radius of a circle fits round the edge of that same circle exactly six times.
So leave the compass at the radius, and put the needle on the top of the circle.
Swing, and it cuts the circle. Move into the cut and swing again.
Walk right round. The sixth one lands exactly where you started.
Join the six points. If it does not close, your compass moved.
The triangle is almost free, once you can do the hexagon.
Step the radius round exactly as before. Six points.
But this time, do not join them all.
Join every other one. Skip, join, skip, join.
Three points instead of six.
That is an equilateral triangle. Three equal sides, and every angle sixty degrees.
Six points, joined two different ways, give you two different shapes.
The square is different, and this catches people out.
You cannot step the radius round for a square. That only gives sixties.
A square needs ninety degrees between its corners.
So take your forty-five degree set square instead.
Draw one diameter at forty-five degrees through the centre.
Then flip it over and draw the other one, crossing at ninety.
Now join the four points where those lines meet the circle.
A square, sitting neatly inside the circle.
Real parts do not have sharp corners. They have rounded ones.
A rounded corner is stronger, and it is safer to handle.
On a drawing we call it a blend, or a fillet, or just a radius.
The arc must flow into the straight line with no kink at all.
The place where they meet is called the tangent point.
Get the tangent points right and the drawing looks professional. Get them wrong and it looks broken.
Start with the easiest case. Two lines meeting at a right angle.
Draw them a little longer than you need.
The extra will be rubbed out at the end, once we know where the arc lands.
The question says join these with a radius of forty.
Here is the rule for every blend on this sheet.
The centre of the arc must be forty away from the first line, and forty away from the second.
So draw a light line forty from the upright one, running parallel to it.
And another forty from the horizontal one.
Where those two light lines cross is the centre.
Now drop back to each line at ninety degrees. Those are your tangent points.
Needle on the centre, and swing from one tangent point to the other.
Then rub out the corner. The arc is the corner now.
Now a corner that is not a right angle. Sixty degrees this time.
Do not panic. The rule has not changed at all.
Draw a light line thirty away from each arm, parallel to it.
Where they cross is the centre.
Perpendicular back to each arm gives the tangent points.
And swing the arc between them.
Notice the tangent points are not the same distance from the corner as before.
That is normal. Never guess them. Always construct them.
Last case, and this is the one the exam likes.
A straight line, a circle, and an arc joining them.
The line part has not changed. The centre must be forty from the line.
Now the circle. The circle has a radius of thirty-two.
Our blend is forty. So the centre must be thirty-two plus forty from the circle centre.
That is seventy-two. Add them together.
So swing an arc of seventy-two from the circle centre, and see where it meets the parallel line.
And here is the last piece. The tangent point on the circle is on the line joining the two centres.
That is always true when two curves touch. Join the centres, and you cross at the touching point.
An ellipse is a squashed circle.
You see one every day. Look at a cup from an angle. The round top looks like an ellipse.
Any circle drawn on a sloping face becomes an ellipse on your paper.
It has two axes. The long way across is the major axis.
The short way is the minor axis.
They cross in the middle, at ninety degrees.
Ours is one hundred and sixty long, and one hundred wide.
Now draw two circles, both on the same centre.
The big one has the major axis as its diameter. So the radius is eighty.
The small one has the minor axis as its diameter. Radius fifty.
Remember, the question gives you the full width, and the compass wants half of it.
These two circles do all the work for us.
Now draw lines out from the centre, straight through both circles.
Every thirty degrees. Your thirty sixty set square gives you all of them.
Twelve lines in total.
If you want a smoother curve, draw more. Every fifteen degrees is better.
Each line cuts the big circle in one place, and the small circle in another.
Here is the clever part. Take one radial line at a time.
From where it cuts the big circle, drop a line straight down.
From where it cuts the small circle, draw a line straight across.
Where those two meet is a point on the ellipse.
Down from the big one. Across from the small one. Do not mix them up.
Now do that for all twelve lines.
Twelve points appear, and you can already see the shape.
Now join the points into a smooth curve.
Do not use a compass. An ellipse is not made of arcs, and it has no one centre.
Use a French curve. Line it up on three or four points at a time.
Draw a little, slide along, and match it to the next points.
Always overlap what you have drawn, or you will leave a kink.
Take your time here. This is the part the examiner looks at.
Second half of the lesson. Scales.
A drawing at one to fifty means everything is fifty times smaller than real life.
You could divide every measurement by fifty. That is slow and you will make mistakes.
So instead we draw a ruler for this one drawing. That is a plain scale.
We want to read up to five metres.
Five metres divided by fifty is one hundred millimetres. So the scale is one hundred long.
Draw a thin box, one hundred by ten.
Then divide it into five equal parts. Each part is one whole metre.
Now the part everybody gets wrong. Where do we write zero?
Not at the left end. Zero goes at the start of the second division.
Everything to the right of zero counts whole metres. One, two, three, four.
And that first division, on the left of zero, gets cut into ten small parts.
Each small part is one tenth of a metre. That is a decimetre.
So to measure three point four metres, you put one leg on the three,
and the other leg four small parts to the left of zero.
Whole units to the right, tenths to the left. Write that down.
Always letter what the scale reads, and always write the ratio underneath.
Here is a solid block. Look at it carefully before you draw anything.
It is like a step. A tall part on the left, and a low part on the right.
It is eighty long, fifty deep, and sixty high.
Now, paper is flat. The block is not flat. So we cannot draw it as it is.
Instead we look at it from three directions, and draw what we see each time.
Look from the front. That gives the front view, or the elevation.
Look from on top, straight down. That gives the plan.
Look from the side. That gives the end view.
Three flat pictures. Together they describe the whole solid, with no guessing.
Before drawing, we decide where each view will sit. This is called setting out.
Beginners skip this, then run out of paper. Do not skip it.
The front view goes here, at the top left.
Now listen, because this is the rule of first angle.
In first angle, the view you get by looking from the top is drawn underneath.
And the view you get by looking from the left is drawn on the right.
It feels backwards at first. It is because the object is pushed away from you.
Leave about thirty millimetres of space between the views, so the drawing can breathe.
Draw these boxes very lightly with your 2H. They are only guides.
We always start with the view that shows the most shape.
Here that is the front view. Looking from the front, the block looks like a letter L.
Start at the bottom left corner and go across. Eighty millimetres.
Now up the right side. Only thirty, because that side is the low part.
Now across to the left, forty. This is the top of the step.
Now up again, thirty more, to reach sixty.
Now across the top, forty, and finally down the left side.
And you are back where you started. That shape is the front view.
Now the plan. And here is the part that saves you time.
You do not measure the plan again. You bring the sizes down from the front view.
Take your set square and drop a light line straight down from every corner.
Down from the left edge.
Down from the step.
And down from the right edge.
These light lines are called projectors. They carry the width downwards.
The width of the plan is now fixed. It must match the front view exactly.
That is the whole idea of projection. The views line up.
Now measure the one size the front view cannot give you. The depth.
The depth is fifty millimetres.
Draw the top line and the bottom line of the plan with your T-square.
Close the two ends on your projectors.
Now one more line. Where the step falls, there is an edge you can see from above.
So draw a full line there, not a dashed one. You can see it, so it is solid.
Your plan is a rectangle, eighty by fifty, with one line across it.
Now we need the end view, on the right.
The heights come across from the front view. That is easy, they are level.
But the depth is in the plan, and the plan is below. The depth is going the wrong way.
So we use a clever line. The mitre line.
Take your forty-five degree set square and draw a line at forty-five degrees.
It starts level with the top of the plan, and under the left of the end view.
What does it do? It bends a measurement round a corner.
A depth measured going down becomes the same depth measured going across.
That is all it is. A corner for measurements to turn on.
Now we feed the end view from two directions.
First, heights. Draw light lines straight across from the front view.
From the bottom, from the step at thirty, and from the top at sixty.
Second, depths. Draw light lines across from the plan until they touch the mitre line.
Where each one touches the mitre line, turn and go straight up.
Across, hit the mitre, turn up. Across, hit the mitre, turn up.
Those upward lines give you the front and the back of the end view.
Now line in the end view, using the crossings you made.
It comes out as a plain rectangle. Fifty wide, and sixty high.
Why a plain rectangle? Because you are looking at the tall part, and it hides the step.
But wait. The step is still there. It is just behind.
And in technical drawing, we never pretend a feature is not there.
So we show it with a dashed line, level with the step, at thirty.
A dashed line means, this edge is there, but you cannot see it from here.
We call it hidden detail. Students forget it and lose easy marks. Do not forget it.
Last part. We put the sizes on, and we name the views.
Dimension lines are thin, with arrowheads touching the projection lines.
The number sits on top of the line, in the middle, and you read it from the bottom or from the right.
Now a rule that catches everybody.
Each size is written once, in one view only. Never twice.
If you put eighty on the front view and eighty on the plan, that is a fault.
Now letter the name under each view. Front view. Plan. End view.
And finally, go over your outlines with the HB so they are black and strong.
Leave the light construction lines. Do not rub them out. They are your working.
That is a complete first angle drawing. Well done.
Last lesson we cut a block into three flat views.
Today we do the opposite. We draw the whole block as one picture.
This is called isometric drawing.
Isometric means equal measure. Iso is equal. Metric is measure.
It has three directions, and only three.
Height goes straight up. Always straight up, never slanted.
Length goes up to the right, at thirty degrees.
Depth goes up to the left, at thirty degrees.
Thirty degrees. That is exactly what your set square gives you, so you never guess.
Start with a dot. This will be the front bottom corner of the block.
It is the corner nearest to your eye.
From that dot, draw a line straight up. That is the height axis.
Now put the thirty sixty set square on your T-square.
Draw a line going up to the right at thirty degrees. That is the length axis.
Now turn the set square over and draw up to the left, also thirty degrees.
Three lines from one corner. That is your frame for everything else.
Now the sizes. And this is the good news.
On these three lines, you measure the real size. No shrinking, no scaling.
Eighty long, so measure eighty along the right hand line.
Fifty deep, so measure fifty along the left hand line.
Sixty high, so measure sixty straight up.
One warning, and it is the biggest mistake in isometric.
You may only measure along these three directions.
Never put your rule on a slanting corner that is not one of the three. That length is false.
Now we build a box. We call it the crate.
Imagine a wooden box that the block fits into exactly, with no space left over.
Eighty by fifty by sixty. Draw it in light construction lines.
Every line is parallel to one of your three axes. There are no other directions.
So slide the set square along and keep drawing parallels.
It is a box in the air. Take your time and it will look solid.
This way of working is called the crating method.
You draw the box first, then you cut pieces off it. Like a carpenter.
Now we cut the step.
The step starts forty millimetres along the length.
Mark that on the bottom front edge, and carry it up the crate.
The step is thirty millimetres high.
Mark thirty up the front corner, and carry it across.
Where those two meet, the piece above and to the right comes off.
Draw the two new faces you have just made.
One face standing up, and one face lying flat.
Now line in. Take the HB and press a little harder.
Go over only the edges you can actually see.
Here is the difference from last lesson.
In orthographic we drew hidden edges as dashed lines.
In isometric we do not. We leave the hidden edges out completely.
There are three of them, and they all meet at the back bottom corner, hiding behind the block.
Your outline should now be dark and clear, standing above the light crate lines.
Look at it. It looks solid. That is why we draw isometric.
One drawing anybody can understand, even someone who cannot read a projection.
Finally, tidy the sheet.
Clean off the loose graphite with a soft eraser or a brush.
Do not rub your construction lines away. They are light, and they belong there.
Never use your hand to sweep the sheet. Your hand leaves a grey smudge.
Letter the title under the drawing.
And fill in the title block in the corner if you have not already.
That is isometric drawing finished.
You now know how to set up a sheet, construct with a compass, and draw a solid two different ways.
Practise each one three times on real paper. The board teaches your hands, not just your head.
Today we draw bars — round bar, square bar and hexagon bar.
A bar is long. Three metres of it will not fit on your sheet.
So we use a convention. We draw both ends, and break out the middle.
The break line says: the part carries on, I have just taken a piece out.
The dimension still says the true length. The drawing is short, the bar is not.
Start with the round bar. Two lines along the T-square, thirty apart.
Close both ends with a short vertical line.
Now put in the centre line, thin and long-short-long.
Here comes the break. Freehand, not with the square.
It waves out one side, back through the middle, and out the other side.
That S is the sign for solid round material. Learn it — it is examined.
Beside it we show the section — what you see if you saw the bar through.
Swing a circle of the same diameter.
Now hatch it. Thin lines at forty-five degrees, evenly spaced.
Hatching must stop on the outline. Never let it run outside the metal.
Solid section, so the hatching goes right across. Nothing is hollow here.
Square bar next, thirty across the flats.
The break is different. Square and flat material takes a zigzag.
One sharp z in the middle of the line, drawn freehand.
The end view is a square, hatched the same forty-five degrees.
Hexagon bar last. This is the material every nut and bolt head is made from.
In the side view it looks like square bar, so we letter it A slash F.
The end view is a true hexagon. Use the thirty-sixty set square.
Across the flats is thirty. Across the corners is bigger — thirty four point six.
The stores will ask you for across flats. Give them that, not the corners.
Last job: the sizes.
Diameter thirty on the round bar. The symbol is a circle with a stroke through it.
Thirty across flats on the square and the hexagon.
And the length — two hundred and fifty — written across the break.
That is the convention working for you. Short drawing, true size.
A tube is a bar with a hole down the middle.
That hole is called the bore.
The metal left round it is the wall.
Outside diameter, take away the bore, divide by two. That is your wall thickness.
Forty outside, twenty-eight bore. Forty take twenty-eight is twelve, halved is six.
Two outside lines, forty apart, along the T-square.
Inside them, two more for the bore.
The bore is inside the metal, so you cannot see it. Draw it hidden — short dashes.
Centre line down the middle, long-short-long.
Close the ends. Now it is a tube, not four lines.
The break on a tube is not one wave. It is one on each wall.
Top wall waves through its own thickness.
Bottom wall does the same.
The gap in the middle is the bore, left open.
Anybody looking at this knows straight away: hollow, and that thick.
Two circles for the end view: outside diameter, then the bore.
Cut it through and you get a ring.
Hatch the ring. Do not hatch the hole.
Hatching in the bore is the commonest mistake in the whole paper.
Outside diameter forty. Bore twenty-eight.
Those two fix everything. The wall is already decided.
If you dimension all three you have over-dimensioned the drawing.
Over-dimensioning loses marks, because two workshops can then argue about which one to work to.
A shaft carries the drive. It turns, so it is round.
It is not one diameter all the way. It is stepped.
Each step is there for something: a bearing here, a gear there.
The face where one step meets the next is called a shoulder.
The shoulder is what stops the bearing sliding along. It locates it.
A round part starts with its centre line. Always.
Long, short, long. Thin. Running past both ends of the part.
Everything else is measured off this line, half a diameter each way.
Twelve above the line and twelve below gives you twenty-four diameter.
Then twenty each way for the forty bearing seat.
Then fifteen each way for the thirty on the output end.
Join the steps with vertical lines. Those are your shoulders.
Leave a gap along the top of the bearing seat. The keyway is cut there.
Never leave a sharp corner on the end of a shaft.
Take a small chamfer with the forty-five set square.
Two by forty-five degrees is the usual one.
It saves fingers, and it helps the shaft start into the bearing.
The gear must not spin on the shaft. So we key it.
A key is a rectangular block sitting half in the shaft, half in the gear.
The slot in the shaft is the keyway.
Draw it on the bearing seat, five deep, and let it break the outline.
And show the end view, so the width and the depth can both be seen.
Diameters first. Twenty-four, then forty, then thirty.
Now the lengths. Take them all from the left-hand face.
That face is the datum. Everything is measured from it.
If you chain the lengths instead, every small error adds to the next one.
From one datum, each length is wrong on its own only. That is why we do it.
A spring is a helix. A helix is a curve going round and along at the same time.
Drawing that curve properly takes an hour and nobody does it.
So the standard says: draw the coils as straight sloping lines.
Everyone reads it as a spring. That is a convention doing its job.
A compression spring is pushed. It gets shorter under load.
First the box the spring lives in.
Centre line down the middle.
Two lines each side for the outside diameter.
Top and bottom lines for the free length — the length with no load on it.
Mean diameter is the middle of the wire. Outside is mean plus one wire.
Now the coils, one pitch apart.
The front of each coil slopes down from left to right.
The back of the same coil comes back the other way.
Front, back, front, back. Six coils here.
Keep every line the same slope. A spring with a wandering pitch looks broken.
Look at the top and bottom coil. They lie flat.
That is called closed and ground.
Closed means the last coil touches the one below it.
Ground means it has been flattened on a wheel so it sits square.
Without that the spring leans over when you press it. It must sit flat.
Free length one hundred and eight.
Outside diameter thirty-nine. Wire diameter five.
And six coils — write that on as a note, you cannot dimension a count.
Those four sizes let anybody wind the same spring again.
A tension spring is pulled. A compression spring is pushed.
That one difference changes the whole drawing.
A pushed spring needs gaps between the coils, so it has somewhere to go.
A pulled spring needs none. Its coils touch when it is at rest.
And it needs something to pull on. That is the loop at each end.
Same sloping lines as before, but no gaps.
The pitch is the wire diameter. Four wire, four pitch.
Fourteen coils, all touching.
It should look tight, like a coil of wire, not like a slinky.
The last coil is turned up to make a loop.
Swing it with the compass so it is a true half circle.
One at each end, both in the same plane.
The loop is where the load goes in — and where the spring breaks first.
Careful with the length on this one.
The free length of a tension spring is measured over the loops.
Not over the coils. Over the loops, outside to outside.
Then outside diameter, wire diameter and the number of coils, same as before.
You already know the key and the keyway.
A spline is the same idea, but many keys, cut into the shaft itself.
Six of them, evenly round the shaft.
Six teeth share the drive, so each one works less and nothing shears off.
And the hub can still slide along, which is exactly what a gearbox needs.
Start the end view with two circles.
The big one is the major diameter — the tips of the splines.
The small one is the minor diameter — the root, the bottom of the spaces.
Sixty and fifty-four. The splines stand three millimetres proud.
Now the teeth. Six of them, sixty degrees apart.
Here is the part people get wrong.
The sides of the tooth are parallel to each other.
They do not point at the centre. They are straight-sided.
Each tooth stands on the root circle and is capped by the major circle.
Along the shaft you do not draw all six splines. Nobody does.
Thick line for the tips, top and bottom.
Thin line just inside it for the roots.
That is the whole convention. Two thick, two thin, and the end view tells the rest.
You cannot dimension six teeth one at a time. Use a note.
Six splines. Major diameter sixty. Minor fifty-four. Width fifteen.
Written once, under the view. That is how the standard wants it.
